help.title: Admin help
help.intro: This guide summarises the admin panel tools, key approval processes, and incident responses. Maintained manually — if something here is wrong, open a PR with a fix rather than leaving the next direction in the dark.

dashboard.title: Dashboard overview
dashboard.p1: /admin — the main page. Four top metrics (users, businesses, events, open reports) + a weekly delta row beneath them.
dashboard.li1: Yellow pill on "Dashboard" in the sidebar — number of items awaiting approval (businesses + reports + flagged products + experiences). Refreshes on every internal navigation.
dashboard.li2: DAU 30-day chart — based on users.last_active_at which updates on every authenticated request (5-min throttle).
dashboard.li3: Top cities — aggregated from producer_page_views (rows without city are not counted).
dashboard.li4: Server health — average response time + requests per minute over the last hour. Per-process only (resets on every deploy).

producers.title: Approving and rejecting businesses
producers.li2: Click the business name → full details page, including licensing declarations, photos, and description.
producers.li3: To approve: click "Quick approve". The business moves to approved, appears on the homepage, and shows on the map.
producers.li4: To reject: "Reject" + a short reason that will be emailed to the business owner.
producers.li5: Edit (pencil): goes to /admin/producers/[id]/edit — all fields including "verified" / "recommended" / "availability status" / "primary contact method".
producers.footnote: A business does not need to be verified to be approved — verified adds a blue tag after you've checked licensing and identity, usually in a monthly audit.

users.title: Managing users
users.p1: /admin/users — search by email/name, filter by role.
users.li1: role: consumer / producer / admin — applied immediately, with no further confirmation.
users.li2: Block: a blocked login returns 403. The user doesn't know immediately, they only see a message on their next login attempt.
users.li3: Favorites: click the count next to a user to see the businesses they saved — useful for tracking suspicious activity.
users.footnote: Reminder: blocking is reversible, a role change affects the next JWT immediately. Do not promote a user to admin without verifying identity outside the system.

reviews.title: Reviews
reviews.p1: /admin/reviews — all reviews in a single list (newest first).
reviews.li1: Filter by rating (1–5) or free-text search across business/user/title/body.
reviews.li2: Deletion requires confirmation (window.confirm). After deletion the business's avg_rating and review count update automatically.
reviews.li3: Deletion is the correct pattern for: defamatory language, personal information, spam, a review about a different business.

reports.title: Reports
reports.li1: Resolve — close the report, optionally with a follow-up action (block / delete).
reports.li2: Hold — keeps it open but moves it to the bottom of the list. Use when more information is needed.
reports.li3: Ignore — close with no action, for reports that don't substantiate an issue.
reports.footnote: Rule of thumb: respond within 24 hours. Product-safety reports (allergens, expiration dates) — immediately.

experiences.title: Experiences
experiences.p1: /admin/experiences — 5 tabs: pending / changes required / approved / rejected / all.
experiences.li1: On click: approve / reject / request changes. The host receives an email.
experiences.li2: Haiku pre-check runs before an experience reaches the "pending" tab — the "changes required" tab is when the AI flagged a warning but did not block.

outreach.title: Business outreach
outreach.p1: /admin/outreach — centralizes leads for potential businesses: contacting, status tracking, and conversion into a registered business.
outreach.li1: Track each lead's status — contacted / pending / converted / rejected.
outreach.li2: Clicking a lead opens its contact details and lets you mark progress.

group_buys.title: Group buys
group_buys.p1: /admin/group-buys — manage users' group buys. The feature is not active right now; the screen is ready for future activation.
group_buys.li1: Once active, open groups and the number of members each has will appear here.
group_buys.li2: Until activation the screen is view-only with no actions.

recipes.title: Recipes
recipes.p1: /admin/recipes — the approval queue for recipes uploaded by users and businesses. Approve, reject, or edit before publishing.
recipes.li1: A pending recipe shows its title, author, and image — check community fit before approving.
recipes.li2: Rejecting removes the recipe from the queue; you can leave a note with the reason.

kashrut.title: Kashrut requests
kashrut.p1: /admin/kashrut — businesses submit requests for a kashrut tag. Approve only after verifying the attached certificate.
kashrut.li1: A pill on "Kashrut" in the sidebar indicates kashrut requests awaiting handling.
kashrut.li2: Approval adds the kashrut tag to the business's public profile.

category_requests.title: Category requests
category_requests.p1: /admin/category-requests — businesses request new categories that don't exist yet. Approve to add them to the list, or reject.
category_requests.li1: Approval creates a new category available to all businesses.
category_requests.li2: Check for duplicates against existing categories before approving.

whatsapp_failures.title: Undelivered messages
whatsapp_failures.p1: /admin/whatsapp-failures — a list of outbound WhatsApp messages that failed to deliver: notifications that never reached businesses.
whatsapp_failures.li1: Check the failure reason (wrong number / block) and reach the business through another channel.
whatsapp_failures.li2: The screen is read-only — no automatic resend from here.

analytics.p1: /admin/analytics — aggregate usage data: active users, top cities, and a breakdown by category.
analytics.li1: Use the charts to track growth trends over time.
analytics.li2: Data updates automatically; no manual action needed.

emergency.title: Emergencies
emergency.site_down_body: Check mehamakor.online/health. If it's not 200 OK, check Railway → healthcheck + logs. See CLAUDE.md §"Railway runtime port = 8080" before any debugging — this is the most common source of 502.
emergency.migration_body: Symptom: the container starts but endpoints return 500 with UndefinedColumn. Fix: verify that _migrate_columns in main.py lists the new column. If not, add it and push a hotfix commit.
emergency.login_broken_body: Verify that JWT_SECRET_KEY exists in Railway Variables. If it was changed by mistake — old JWTs are invalidated and every user has to log in again. Do not rotate the key without alerting the team.
emergency.spam_body: /register/producer is already rate-limited to 3/hour (slowapi). If that isn't enough, tighten to 1/hour temporarily in auth.py + hotfix push. Block suspicious IPs at Railway edge if traffic is unusual.

story.p1: It was always important to me to know where my food comes from. I wanted to buy better — healthier, more local.
story.p2: But I quickly discovered that it isn't accessible. To find truly good food, I had to search for hours — asking the right people, joining WhatsApp groups, searching on Google and Instagram.

eggs.question: Why are organic eggs worth the price?
eggs.answer: Organic hens grow up outdoors, eating food free of pesticides and antibiotics. Their eggs contain more omega-3, vitamin E, and antioxidants. Not a dramatic difference — but less exposure to chemicals, and more humane lives for the hens.

grass_fed.question: What is grass-fed in Israel?
grass_fed.answer: At the supermarket — most cattle are fattened on corn and supplements. Grass-fed = cows that lived their whole lives in pasture, eating natural grass. In Israel it's rare and more expensive — but the meat has deeper flavor, the distinctive yellowish fat, and more omega-3. Producers like Gilis from the Golan Heights and Mireh Golan are classic examples.

honey.question: Supermarket honey vs. unheated honey — what's the difference?
honey.answer: Supermarket honey is pasteurized — heating destroys enzymes, antioxidants, and pollen. Unheated honey keeps it all — richer flavor, natural antibacterial properties. How to spot it? Thicker, not completely clear, sometimes crystallizes — and that's a good sign.

about_business.heading: Frequently-asked questions for business owners

cost.q: How much does it cost to sign up?
cost.a: Zero. You don't pay us anything — no order commission, no subscription fee. Customers reach you directly on WhatsApp or by phone, and you keep 100% of their payment.

value.q: What do I get out of it?
value.a:
Two things you didn't have before:

**That people will find you on Google.** Someone searching Google for local food — finds you. Today, if you're not buying an ad budget, you're nearly invisible. With us every business gets a page that ranks in search.

**A stable page that doesn't disappear.** Instagram disappears after 24 hours. WhatsApp disappears when someone isn't in the group. Your page on Mehamakor — stays. With your story, your photos, and the contact channels you choose. You can share it as a link and put it in your Instagram bio.

time.q: How long will this take me?
time.a: About 10 minutes for the initial setup. After that — you don't manage anything else with us. You keep working the way you work. If something changes — opening hours, a new product, a break — you update it with one tap, or send me a message on WhatsApp and I'll update.

writing.q: I don't know how to write about myself. Will the page look thin?
writing.a: You don't have to write it alone. Tell me about your business in whatever way you usually write — WhatsApp, Instagram, however is comfortable — and I'll help phrase it. Phone photos are great, you don't need a professional photographer. If you want — we can spend 15 minutes on the phone and build it together.

founder.a: I'm Sapir, 21, from Zikhron Ya'akov. I built Mehamakor because I was also looking for places to buy real, local food, and it was hard — WhatsApp groups, Instagram searches. I wanted one place. I'm on my own for now, no investors, no big company. You can talk to me on WhatsApp directly and ask anything you want.

leads.q: The customers who arrive through you — yours or mine?
leads.a: Yours. Completely. Customers reach out to you directly on WhatsApp or by phone — you get their details, you manage the relationship. We're not in the middle, we don't see the messages, we don't take their info. Even if Mehamakor closed tomorrow, the customers who reached you through us stay yours. It's the opposite of Wolt or Yango.

visibility.q: I'm already on Instagram and WhatsApp — why do I need another place?
visibility.a:
Instagram only works when someone already follows you. WhatsApp groups only work when someone is already in the group. Mehamakor works even when you're not thinking about it — someone searching Google for local food finds you. It's not instead of your channels, it's in addition.

And it matters to know — on Mehamakor there is no comparison. No prices side by side, no star ratings, no "see 10 similar businesses" button. Each business stands on its own. The customer sees you, not you-versus-others.

control.q: I want to decide who I work with and when.
control.a: You decide when you're open. One button — "Taking orders," "Busy right now," "On a break" — you pick. No one ranks you by how fast you replied. You reply on WhatsApp only when you want to. And if a customer isn't right for you — you don't have to. There's no rating that drops if you say "Sorry, not this time."

body.b0: There's one field on your profile page on Mehamakor that changes everything: **the description**.
body.b1: A new customer arriving at your page through Mehamakor sees the first photo, then the first 2-3 lines of text. What's written there decides whether she keeps reading or goes back to the search page.
body.b2: On other food sites, this field is a place to list products. On Mehamakor it's different. Mehamakor isn't built like a marketplace — it's built to give every business a full page, with photos, a map, and a story. **The story is the reason someone will remember you two weeks from now.**
body.b4: Why a story — and not a product list?
body.b5: Because **products sell one transaction. A story sells the return.**
body.b6: A customer who read your story — how you started, why you chose the category, what's special about your approach — will remember you. Will tell a friend. Will come back in a month. A customer who only saw a product list bought once, if at all, and forgot.
body.b7: That's not an opinion. That's how human memory works. Numbers take up short-term memory. Stories get etched in.
body.b9: Three questions that build a good story
body.b10: Before you open the description field — take 10 minutes and answer these questions. In writing, for real. Don't skip this.
body.b12: Not "why I opened a business" — that's the generic answer everyone gives ("I wanted to be independent," "I always loved the field"). Rather: **what made you choose this category specifically?**

b13.i0: Baker? Was there a moment you realized supermarket bread isn't enough?
b13.i1: Farmer? Studied agriculture in the US? Inherited from your grandfather?
b13.i2: Vintner? Tasted a specific wine that made you think "I can make better than this"?

body.b14: **The first moment** — that's what makes a story.
body.b16: Not relative to competitors. **Relative to the baseline in the category.**
body.b17: If you bake bread, you're not comparing yourself to another baker. You're comparing yourself to the average bread someone can buy at the supermarket. What's the difference?

b18.i0: Organic flour from a specific mill?
b18.i2: The oven your late grandfather worked on?

body.b19: Specificity. **One specific thing with details** beats 5 generic claims ("high quality, fresh, local").
body.b20: **3. Who are you making this for?**
body.b21: Not "for everyone." That's an answer that speaks to no one.
body.b22: Think of one real customer who bought from you in the last month. Picture her. You're writing to her. If you run a sourdough bakery — maybe she's the mother of a child with a digestive sensitivity to regular bread, and sourdough is the only one that works for him. If you run a small dairy — maybe it's a couple paying a premium for milk because they believe in ethical farming.
body.b23: When you know who — the text writes itself.
body.b28: Galit's Bread Bakery — a quality boutique bakery. We specialize in sourdough breads, pastries, and pita bread. All our products are from organic flour, premium quality. Order now!

b30.i1: "All products from organic flour" — doesn't say which flour, from where

body.b32: Galit started baking in 2019, after a year at a bakery in France. The first loaf came out burnt. Two years later, she opened the bakery. The flour comes from a small mill in the north — organic, milled the day it reaches her. 36-hour fermentation. A small bakery, 4 loaves a day. If you came late — come back tomorrow.

b34.i1: Regional details (France, north) → sense of place without inventing fake businesses
b34.i4: "If you came late — come back tomorrow" → personality

body.b40: "Karmiel" beats "the north." "A mill at Kibbutz X" beats "local flour." Specifics = credibility. (Just make sure you're using real names — customers will check.)
body.b42: "Since 2019" helps a customer know you're not brand-new. Even if you are new — "since June 2024" beats nothing.
body.b44: No more. The first story is just the opening. The rest of the details go to the full "about" page or the product catalog.
body.b45: **5. Read it out loud before you save.**
body.b46: If it sounds like an ad — start over. If it sounds like you're telling a friend — you're ready.

b49.i0: **Don't:** Don't open with "Welcome." That's wasted space. Use it for the story.
b49.i1: **Don't:** Don't write in passive voice. "We believe..." or "I started in 2019..." beats "The company was founded in 2019..."
b49.i2: **Don't:** Don't mention competitors. "Better than X" signals insecurity.
b49.i3: **Don't:** Don't promise things you can't prove. "The best product in the area" — you can be sued for that.
b49.i4: **Don't:** No emojis in the text. For emphasis use a heading, bold, or italics — not emojis.

body.b52: If you're sitting in front of the field and can't get started — write to me. I'll read the story, point out where it's strong and where it's weak, and help edit. **Free, personal, but it takes me a few days — I work with every business by myself.**
body.b53: This isn't an offer for everyone. It's an option for new business owners who don't yet know what it looks like. After you've written it once — you'll always know.

product_photography.title: How to photograph your products properly
product_photography.subtitle: No professional camera. No studio. On the phone you already have.
product_photography.preview: 5 principles + a 30-minute workflow. How to produce 15 quality photos for the profile using your phone.

body.b0: On your profile page on Mehamakor, **the first photo is the moment a customer decides whether to stay**. Before they read the story. Before they see the price. Before everything.
body.b1: And yet — many business owners open the upload field, look at the photos on their phone, and feel they're "not professional enough." They upload one photo from their Instagram from two years ago, and hope for the best.
body.b2: This is the guide that explains why you don't need to shoot in a studio, and what you do need.
body.b4: The first rule: you don't need a professional camera
body.b6: Professional shots of boutique bakeries you see on Instagram — a large share of them were shot on a phone. The difference isn't the gear. The difference is:
body.b12: Flash flattens the photo and turns food into plastic. A ceiling bulb creates harsh shadows from above. Direct noon sun does the same.

b14.i0: Natural light through a window, between 9:00-11:00 a.m. or 15:00-17:00
b14.i1: Overcast days — actually excellent. Diffuse, soft light

body.b15: **Simple technique:** place the product next to a window — light should fall from the side, not from above and not facing you. You'll see the side near the window is bright and the other side in light shadow — that's exactly what you want.
body.b18: This is the tip that works hardest, and business owners are the most embarrassed by it.
body.b19: **The strongest photo on your profile is you, with the products, in your hands.** Not a professional portrait in an office. You at work. In work clothes. With flour on your hands. With fruit in a basket.

b21.i0: **People buy from people.** Seeing a face → feeling trust.
b21.i1: **This is what Mehamakor is.** Not a transactional platform, a place that shows who's behind every business.
b21.i2: **Big chains can't show the "owner at work." You can.**

b23.i0: A farmer holding vegetables she just picked
b23.i1: A baker pulling bread out of the oven
b23.i2: A dairy farmer next to the cows during milking
b23.i3: A vintner looking at grapes in the vineyard

body.b26: Most business owners only photograph **the finished product**. But the customer also wants to see how it was made.
body.b27: **The simple method:** think about a regular workday at your place. From start to finish. **3 moments worth a photo:**

b28.i0: **The preparation moment** — before the product is ready. The raw ingredients, the equipment, the first hand that touches it.
b28.i1: **The transformation moment** — when the raw material becomes a product. (It's different in every category — but it's always there.)
b28.i2: **The finishing moment** — the product is ready. A moment before it leaves the business.

body.b29: **A 5-minute exercise:** take a piece of paper. Write your day in your business in one line — from morning to end. Mark 3 points where there's something to see. They don't have to be pretty, they have to be real. Next time that day happens — shoot the 3 points.
body.b30: **Why it works:** the customer sees what's actually happening, not only the polished end result. **Process = transparency = trust.**
body.b33: Your place is part of the story.

b34.i0: A farm in the Galilee → let the Galilee show in the photos
b34.i1: A bakery in Tel Aviv → photograph the street from outside
b34.i2: A dairy in the Negev → the Negev landscape is part of your story

body.b35: **Tip:** don't be afraid of "background noise" — an old wooden crate, a linen tablecloth, an empty bench. It's not distracting. It **gives the photo character**. The opposite of a stock photo.
body.b40: **The reason:** a filter changes the product's color. The customer will get the product at home and see something else. Disappointment = bad review = customer who doesn't come back.
body.b44: For every main product in your catalog — shoot at least 3 photos:

b45.i0: **The product alone** — on a wood surface, a linen cloth, or a simple background. No over-styling. Just the product.
b45.i1: **The product in a hand** — your hand, a customer's hand, a hand holding the product. **Scale** (size relative to a hand) plus **human life**.
b45.i2: **The product in context** — on a dining table, next to a coffee cup, in the shipping packaging, in a gift box. **Real use.**

b49.i0: A baker holding warm bread, you can see the crust, natural light from the window
b49.i1: A farmer in the vineyard holding a cluster of grapes, with evening sky behind
b49.i2: A hand touching a jar of yogurt, you can see the thick texture

b51.i0: A product on a sterile white background (Amazon vibes)
b51.i1: An overhead flatlay that's too tidy (Pinterest vibes)
b51.i2: A glossy macro with dripping sauce (aggressive food styling)
b51.i4: Industrial packaging under studio lighting (Whole Foods vibes)

body.b52: Mehamakor's style: **like a photo a close friend would take when she came to visit your business, not like a brand-shot paid for by a professional photographer.**
body.b55: If you have 30 free minutes in the morning, here's how you'll get a solid set of photos:

b56.i0: **Pick 5 products** from the catalog. The most important to you.
b56.i1: **Find a window** in your kitchen / business with nice side light.
b56.i2: **For each product** — shoot 20 photos. 3 angles × a few takes each.
b56.i3: **Come back later** and pick the 3 best for each product.

body.b57: That's it. 15 photos for the profile — more than 90% of the businesses on the site have.
body.b59: What if I don't have good photos right now?

b61.i0: **Use a placeholder until you shoot** — Mehamakor shows a small category icon instead of a missing photo. Not attractive, but not invisible.
b61.i1: **Schedule one short shoot** — if you have half a day free, shoot everything at once. A few hours of watching the light = many photos.
b61.i2: **Hire a local photographer** — sometimes worth the investment. A local photographer can give you many quality photos in half a day. Prices vary — ask for 2-3 quotes before deciding. If you're in for the year — it's a worthwhile investment.

body.b64: Send me 2-3 photos you've taken. I'll look and explain which one works, which doesn't, and why. **Free, personal, but it takes me a few days — I work with every business by myself.**
body.b65: It's not a regular service — it's an option for new business owners still learning what works.

customer_messages.title: How to reply to messages from customers
customer_messages.subtitle: Response time, tone, and what to write when you don't know what to write.
customer_messages.preview: The small things that decide between a conversation ending in an order and one ending in "I'll get back to you." 5 principles + 5 ready-made templates.

body.b0: The first message from a new customer is a small moment that decides a lot.
body.b1: The person writing to you doesn't know you personally. Doesn't know if you'll reply. Doesn't know if you're serious. **The first three lines you send back decide whether they keep going, or look elsewhere.**
body.b2: This guide isn't about being "polite" or "professional." It's about the small things that make a real difference between a conversation that ends in an order and a conversation that ends with "thanks, I'll get back to you" that never comes back.
body.b4: The first rule: response time matters more than the response itself
body.b5: A woman writes to you in the evening. Asks about a product. Looking for confirmation that you're available, that the product exists, that you're serious.
body.b6: If she didn't get a reply by the next afternoon — she's **already looked elsewhere**. Not because your product is less good. But because **she doesn't know you're still there**.
body.b7: This is the most important rule: **fast response > perfect response.**
body.b11: Not instant — you're a business owner, not a chatbot. But within 4 hours during working hours, **reply with something**.

b13.i0: "Hi, saw your message. I'll reply with details this evening."
b13.i1: "Thanks for reaching out! I'm at work right now, I'll get back to you within two hours."
b13.i2: "Got your message. Just finishing a delivery, I'll be free at 14:00."

body.b14: This isn't a full reply. It's an **acknowledgement**. A customer who knows you saw the message waits. A customer who doesn't know — leaves.
body.b17: Message came in at 22:00? Don't feel obligated to reply immediately. But **one line in the morning changes everything**:
body.b18: Good morning! Saw your message last night. Replying in detail now.
body.b19: **The reason:** the customer woke up and opened her phone. If the first thing she saw was a reply from you — you'll be on her mind all day.
body.b20: **Another tip:** set a WhatsApp status with your business hours:
body.b21: Active 9:00-17:00. I reply to every message in the morning.
body.b22: This doesn't replace a personal reply — it sets expectations before someone writes.
body.b24: **3. Personal beats template. But not completely.**
body.b26: **The first extreme:** an over-formatted reply. "Greetings. Thank you for your inquiry. The full catalog will be sent in a separate file. For any further questions, please email us."
body.b27: **The problem:** the customer feels like she's talking to a robot. Or to a company that doesn't have time.
body.b28: **The second extreme:** a completely ad-libbed reply. "Hi Dana! How fun that you asked. So we make pita every day at 6 in the morning, we have 3 kinds — whole wheat, regular, and a new green pita with zaatar we just tried this week and it really came out tasty, if you want I can send you a photo..."
body.b29: **The problem:** it takes you 10 minutes per message. Not sustainable.

b31.i0: **Personal opening** ("Hi Dana! Thanks for reaching out.") — one line, personal.
b31.i1: **Body of the message in a template** (catalog, price list, delivery times) — what repeats.
b31.i2: **Personal closing** ("Looking forward to your order — message when you're ready.") — one line, personal.

body.b34: This is the tip that changes the closing rate.
body.b36: **Don't — The poor approach:** sending the whole catalog right away. 12 cheeses, prices, descriptions. The customer sees a wall of text and closes the chat.
body.b37: **Do — The good approach:** asking one question. "Yes! For dinner for two, or hosting a group? I have different recommendations for each."

b39.i0: **Starts a conversation** instead of closing it.
b39.i1: **Makes the customer feel cared for.** She didn't get a catalog — she got attention.
b39.i2: **Shortens the decision.** After she replies "dinner for two" — you have 2-3 cheeses to recommend, not 12.

body.b40: **The rule:** before you send information — ask **one focused question** that helps narrow it down.
body.b42: **5. A conversation doesn't have to end in a sale.**
body.b43: Sometimes a customer asks and doesn't buy. Asks for a price list, explores options, then goes quiet. That's fine.
body.b44: **The reason:** a good reply today = an order in 3 months. Or a recommendation to a friend. Or a return when the situation changes.
body.b45: If you try to "close at all costs" — asking "so what did you decide?", pushing, offering — you **lose those 3 months**.
body.b46: **What to do after a conversation that didn't end in an order:**

b47.i0: Send a short thanks. "Thanks for asking! If you need anything in the future, I'm here."
b47.i1: **Don't** follow up a week later. **Don't** remind them of yourself again "by chance." **Don't** send a newsletter if they didn't ask for one.

body.b48: The customer knows where to find you. If she wants to — she'll come back.
body.b51: Save these in WhatsApp Business (the "quick replies" feature) or in a note on your phone. To save time:
body.b53: Hi [name]! Got your message. I'll reply in detail within [X] hours.
body.b54: **2. Filtering question (customer asks "what do you have?"):**
body.b55: One short question — what are you looking for? [two options to pick from]. That way I know what to recommend.
body.b57: Sending the price list Delivery to your area [X] NIS. Delivery within [Z] days. Tell me what to pick and I'll prepare.
body.b59:
Great! Got your order. I'll prepare [details].
[If pickup:] Come pick up on [day, time] at [address].
[If delivery:] Delivery on [day] for [Y] NIS.
body.b60: **5. Closing a conversation that didn't end in an order:**
body.b61: Thanks for asking! If you need anything in the future — I'm here.

b64.i0: **Don't:** Don't apologize if you replied within the standard (4 hours during work hours). An apology creates the impression of "I hurt something." If you replied in a reasonable time — give a direct reply without "sorry that..."
b64.i1: **Don't:** Don't send a "?" if the customer hasn't replied. It feels pressured. Send a full sentence or nothing.
b64.i2: **Don't:** Don't post private customer messages in WhatsApp statuses — even without a name. Others will see it, understand that you share private chats, and won't write to you.
b64.i3: **Don't:** Don't write in all caps. In English it's shouting. In Hebrew it reads as angry.
b64.i4: **Don't:** Don't send 5 separate messages ("Hi" → "I saw" → "Give me a minute" → "I'm at work" → "I'll get back later"). Send one complete message.

body.b67: Have a message you don't know how to reply to? **Send me a screenshot** (without the customer's identifying details — blur the name and phone). I'll reply with how I'd write it. **Free, personal, but it takes me a few days — I work with every business by myself.**
body.b68: It's not a regular service — it's an option for new business owners still learning the rhythm.

hero.h1: Every business here goes through us — a personal introduction.
hero.sub: Before a business goes live, we get to know the person behind it — we hear the story, understand how they work, and sometimes we come to visit.

steps.lead: Four steps, one person on the other side. This is how it works from the request to going live.
steps.s1_body: It all starts with a short form — what's made, from which ingredients, and where. Every request is read by a person, from the very first word.
steps.s2_body: A personal conversation — on WhatsApp or by phone. Who stands behind the business, what a workday looks like, and where the raw ingredients come from.
steps.s3_body: Sometimes we travel. When it helps us understand the place — we come to see the kitchen, the farm, or the hive with our own eyes.
steps.s4_body: We've gotten to know them, there's a fit — the business goes live. That's it: now you can find it and message it directly.
steps.badge_aside_title: The "Verified" badge is a separate step — and optional
steps.badge_aside_body: It's added when an official licensing or exemption document is submitted, and we review it. Without the badge, the business is still here — and still went through the same personal introduction as everyone else.

everyone.intro: No matter the category and no matter whether there's a badge — these three things are checked for everyone, always.
everyone.c1_body: Who stands behind the business. A real name and place. No anonymity.
everyone.c2_body: How and why they work this way. What goes into the product — and what doesn't.
everyone.c3_body: We talked. A person across from us, not a form that approved itself.

badge.oneliner: The "Verified" badge says one thing: an official licensing or exemption document was submitted — and we reviewed it.
badge.absence_h3: No verified badge? It doesn't mean less
badge.absence_body: Some categories are legally exempt from licensing — they have no document to show, simply because none is required. Such a business is "Declared": a binding declaration of lawful operation was signed, and the business went through the same personal introduction as everyone else.
badge.absence_kicker: The badge marks an extra document — not extra trust.

matrix.intro: We don't hide the criteria. Here, by category, is the document that earns the "Verified" badge — and when "Declared" is exactly the right path.
matrix.groupA_title: Categories where the law requires a license
matrix.groupA_desc: Here the law requires a license — so here there's always an official document (from the local authority or the Ministry of Health) that was submitted and reviewed. Without a valid license, the business simply doesn't go live.
matrix.honey_doc: Three licenses together — beekeeper, marketing, and business. One alone isn't enough.
matrix.groupB_desc: Here the law exempts from licensing. Most businesses will be "Declared" — a full path in its own right. Whoever wishes can add an exemption approval or registration and also receive a "Verified" badge.
matrix.caveat: Our process is personal, and the criteria update with the law and with new categories. If something isn't clear — talk to us, and we'll explain.

vegetables.label: Vegetables
vegetables.doc: Verified: an exemption approval from the local authority.
vegetables.declare: Declared: a declaration that this is self-grown produce.

fruits.label: Fruits
fruits.doc: Verified: an exemption approval from the local authority.
fruits.declare: Declared: a declaration that this is self-grown produce.

oils.label: Olive oil & oils
oils.doc: Verified: an official exemption approval from the business-licensing department.

soaps.label: Natural soaps
soaps.doc: Verified: registration in the cosmetics registry (Ministry of Health).

creams.label: Skin creams & oils
creams.doc: Verified: registration in the cosmetics registry.

candles.label: Candles & aroma
candles.note: In this category there's no path to a badge — there's simply no document to verify, and that's perfectly fine.

closing.quote: I want to know who I'm buying from. I built a place where you know too.

cta.h2: Have a business that deserves a home?
cta.intro: Tell us about it. We'll read it, get back to you, and start getting to know you.
